input.question: If the Hubble telescope can zoom into the far reaches of the galaxy, why can't we just point it at Earth-like planets to see if they have water/vegetation etc.
input.ground_truth: We can't "see" earth like planets. They are too far away. The hubble telescope is great for seeing faint and far away things. We can see faint stars. We can see distant galaxies. We can see BOTH of these things because they give off light. We point our telescope at these and basically "leave the shutter open". This gathers light over an extended period of time. **Planets do not give off light. They only reflect light. This is not enough light to actually "see" the planet itself.** And on the remote chance we do see it, it isn't in enough detail to see the surface. The reason we know planets exist is not because we "see" them. It is because we see the effect they have on the stars they orbit.

Question: If the Hubble telescope can zoom into the far reaches of the galaxy, why can't we just point it at Earth-like planets to see if they have water/vegetation etc.

Okay, imagine you have a really, really powerful magnifying glass. This magnifying glass is so strong, it can see things super far away, like stars and galaxies very, very far from us.

But if you want to look at something really tiny and close, like a small ant on the ground, the magnifying glass isn’t good for that. It’s only good at seeing things that are super far away, not things that are close and small.

Now, Earth-like planets are like tiny dots in the sky. They are so far away that even the Hubble telescope can only see them as tiny specks, not as big pictures where you can see if there are trees or water. It’s like trying to see if a tiny dot on the wall is a picture of a tree or just a dot – you can’t tell with a magnifying glass that only sees far things.

So, we need special ways, like other kinds of telescopes or clever tricks with light, to learn if those faraway dots have things like water or plants.
